name: Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary
tagline: Rhododendron and fir forest on the Tsomgo road
meta_description: Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary guide: rhododendron season, blood pheasant and red panda habitat, permits, altitude and how to see it on the Tsomgo road.
summary: Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary covers about 31 sq km of fir, juniper and rhododendron forest between roughly 3,290 m and 4,120 m, around 31 km from Gangtok on the road to Tsomgo Lake. Most visitors see it from the road; April and May bring the rhododendrons, and birders come for the blood pheasant.
intro: Set up in 1977, Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary wraps around the road to Tsomgo Lake and covers about 31 sq km. It starts roughly 31 km from Gangtok, where the road climbs out of mixed forest into silver fir, juniper and rhododendron. The altitude ranges from about 3,290 m to about 4,120 m, with steep cliffs that hold snow for much of the year.

For most travellers, Kyongnosla is the forest you drive through on the way to Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La. Look out of the window in April and May, when rhododendrons flower red, pink and cream between the firs, and in early summer, when waterfalls spill onto the road. The ground flora includes primulas, irises, aconites, potentillas, ground orchids and wild strawberries.

The sanctuary protects habitat for the red panda, in the bamboo thickets lower down, and for pheasants including the Himalayan monal and the blood pheasant, Sikkim's state bird. BirdLife lists it, with Tsomgo and the Cho La area, as an Important Bird Area. Walks off the road need forest department permission and a local guide; ask us before you plan one.

story.title: Where Sikkim's state bird lives outside the park
story.text: The blood pheasant, Ithaginis cruentus, is Sikkim's state bird: a plump, crested pheasant whose males are streaked grey with splashes of crimson on the face, throat and tail. It lives in fir and rhododendron forest close to the tree line, moving down in winter snow. Most of its Sikkim range lies inside Khangchendzonga National Park, far from any road. Kyongnosla is different. According to BirdLife's Important Bird Area assessment, the Kyongnosla–Tsomgo–Tamze–Cho La complex is the site outside the national park where the blood pheasant is found, probably in significant numbers. That makes this roadside sanctuary, an hour and a half from the capital, one of the easiest places in India to look for the state bird. The same assessment notes that grazing once used the open areas in summer, until the government banned grazing in forest areas. If you are lucky, a small flock will be scratching in the snow beside the road on a winter morning.
story.source: BirdLife International IBA factsheet: Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary–Tsomgo–Tamze–Chola Complex; Wikipedia: Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary

little_known.fact: Kyongnosla was declared a sanctuary in 1977 and is part of WWF's Sacred Himalayan Landscape, a conservation corridor running from Nepal through Sikkim to Bhutan.
The sanctuary's dense bamboo thickets at lower altitudes are classic red panda habitat, though the animal is shy and rarely seen from the road.
little_known.source: BirdLife IBA factsheet; Sikkim forest department material

little_known.fact: Kyongnosla's ground flora includes aconites, potentilla, asters, irises, ground orchids and wild strawberries, flowering mostly from May to August.

highlights.title: Rhododendrons in April and May
highlights.text: As the road climbs above about 3,000 m, rhododendron trees and shrubs bloom among the silver firs, from deep red to pink and cream. Peak flowering shifts with altitude and the year, usually from mid-April to late May. Ask your driver to stop at a safe pull-out.

highlights.title: Blood pheasant country
highlights.text: Sikkim's state bird lives here near the tree line, and winter mornings sometimes bring small flocks to the roadside snow. Keep binoculars handy, stay in or beside the car and keep quiet. A local birding guide improves your chances considerably.

highlights.title: Fir, juniper and old forest
highlights.text: Tall silver firs, gnarled junipers and rhododendrons hung with lichen make Kyongnosla one of the most accessible high-altitude forests in Sikkim. In mist the forest is eerie and beautiful; in sun it smells of resin.

highlights.title: Waterfalls on the road
highlights.text: In May and June, snowmelt and early rain send streams and small waterfalls down the cliffs onto the road. They are pretty but can loosen rocks; drivers slow down and keep moving. Photograph them only from safe spots.

highlights.title: Alpine flowers in summer
highlights.text: From May to August the ground flora comes out: primulas, irises, aconites, potentillas and ground orchids. This is also monsoon season, with cloud and landslide risk, so flower lovers should plan carefully and keep spare days.

how_to_reach.text: Kyongnosla lies on the Tsomgo road, so shared Tsomgo and Baba Mandir tours from Gangtok pass through it, for about ₹800–1,200 a seat. Shared tours rarely stop for long in the sanctuary, so they suit casual viewing rather than birding or photography.

A reserved car for Tsomgo and Baba Mandir costs about ₹4,500–6,500 and lets you stop at safe pull-outs in the sanctuary. For a birding morning, we arrange an early start with a local guide and forest permission. The sanctuary begins about 31 km from Gangtok, roughly 1.5 hours away.

Kyongnosla is reached only from Gangtok, on the protected road to Tsomgo, with permits arranged a day ahead. Spend at least one night in Gangtok first. NH10 from the plains closes in the monsoon; check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: There is no tourist accommodation inside the sanctuary. Stay in Gangtok and visit on the Tsomgo day trip or on an early birding morning. The Hidden Forest Retreat at Sichey, with its orchid garden, suits nature lovers; Hotel Tibet and The Chumbi Residency are central for early pickups, and Mintokling Guest House and Hotel Sonam Delek suit budget travellers.
tips: Bring binoculars and keep them in your lap, not in the boot; birds appear suddenly near the road.
Ask your driver to stop only at safe pull-outs; Army convoys use this road.
Do not pick flowers or dig up plants; this is a protected area.
Walks off the road need forest department permission and a guide; arrange it in advance.
Mid-April to late May is the safest bet for rhododendrons, but timing varies with the year.

experiences.title: Rhododendron drive through Kyongnosla
experiences.cost: Included in the Tsomgo car hire
experiences.summary: In spring, the Tsomgo road through Kyongnosla becomes one of the easiest rhododendron drives in Sikkim, with red, pink and cream blooms between silver firs above about 3,000 m. Plan a private car so you can stop at the right places.
body: Sikkim has dozens of rhododendron species, and several grow along the Tsomgo road, from tree-sized species lower down to shrubs near the lake. From about mid-April to late May, depending on the year and the altitude, they flower in waves: lower slopes first, higher ones later. Kyongnosla's fir forest makes a dark backdrop for the colour.

A private car lets you stop at safe pull-outs and walk a few metres along the road. Do not climb the banks, pick flowers or break branches: the area is protected, and the slopes are loose. Early morning light is best, before cloud builds. On the way back down, the afternoon light can also be good.

Combine the drive with Tsomgo and Baba Mandir on the usual permit. If the high road is closed for snow, rhododendrons may still be visible lower down. Keep a spare day. For a longer rhododendron trip, look at Barsey in Soreng district or Yumthang and Shingba in North Sikkim.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom on the Tsomgo road?
faqs.a: Usually from about mid-April to late May, starting lower and moving up the mountain. The exact timing shifts by a week or two with each year's weather. Early May is often a safe middle point. Check current status before you travel and ask us for recent reports.

faqs.q: Can we stop to photograph rhododendrons in Kyongnosla?
faqs.a: Yes, at safe pull-outs, with a private car. Shared tours rarely stop. Do not stop on blind bends, as Army convoys use the road, and do not climb the banks or pick flowers. Your driver knows the places where stopping is allowed.

faqs.q: Is Kyongnosla better than Yumthang for rhododendrons?
faqs.a: Yumthang and the Shingba Rhododendron Sanctuary in North Sikkim have larger and more famous displays, but need a two-night North Sikkim permit trip. Kyongnosla is easier, as it lies on the Tsomgo day trip from Gangtok. For a short trip, Kyongnosla is the practical choice.

experiences.title: Early birding for the blood pheasant
experiences.summary: An early-morning birding trip into Kyongnosla with a local guide, looking for Sikkim's state bird, the blood pheasant, as well as monals and high-altitude finches. One of the few places outside the national park where the blood pheasant is reliably recorded.
body: BirdLife's Important Bird Area assessment singles out the Kyongnosla–Tsomgo area as the site outside Khangchendzonga National Park where the blood pheasant is found, probably in good numbers. The birds move down to lower slopes in winter snow, which makes November to April the best time to look, and early morning the best time of day.

We start from Gangtok before sunrise with a local birding guide and the required permits. The guide knows the stretches of road and forest edge where flocks feed. Stay in or beside the car, move slowly and keep voices low. Other species to look for include the Himalayan monal, grandala, rosefinches and laughingthrushes.

Sightings are never guaranteed. Combine the morning with Tsomgo, which you reach as the day warms up. Walking off the road inside the sanctuary needs forest department permission, which we arrange in advance. Dress for sub-zero temperatures at dawn and carry hot drinks. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where can we see the blood pheasant in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Most of its Sikkim range is inside Khangchendzonga National Park, far from roads. The Kyongnosla–Tsomgo area on the road to Nathu La is the main accessible site outside the park, according to BirdLife. Winter and early spring mornings, with a local guide, give the best chance.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit for birding in Kyongnosla?
faqs.a: Driving the road needs the Tsomgo protected-area permit, arranged a day ahead. Walking into the forest off the road needs permission from the Sikkim forest department and a local guide. We arrange both for birding trips. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What other birds can we see near Tsomgo?
faqs.a: Besides the blood pheasant, look for the Himalayan monal, grandala, snow pigeon, rosefinches, accentors and laughingthrushes, depending on season and altitude. A local guide helps with identification and locations. Winter brings some species lower; summer brings breeding birds higher up.

experiences.title: Alpine flowers of Kyongnosla in summer
experiences.summary: From May to August, Kyongnosla's ground flora flowers: primulas, irises, aconites, potentillas, asters and ground orchids. A trip for plant lovers who accept monsoon cloud and keep a flexible plan.
body: Once the snow melts, the open slopes and forest edges of Kyongnosla fill with small flowers. BirdLife and forest department records list aconites, potentilla, asters, irises, ground orchids and wild strawberries among the ground flora, alongside primulas that flower soon after the snow retreats. Some of these plants grow only in the high Himalaya.

This is monsoon season, so expect cloud, rain and short clear spells. Mornings are usually best. Travel with a private car and a local guide who knows the plants and the safe stopping places. Walking into the sanctuary needs forest department permission; roadside viewing does not.

Do not pick, uproot or collect any plant: aconites in particular are poisonous, and collecting is illegal in the sanctuary. Landslides can close the road at short notice in July and August. Keep spare days in Gangtok and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it safe to visit Kyongnosla in the monsoon?
faqs.a: The Tsomgo road usually stays open in the monsoon, but landslides and cloud are common, especially in July and August. Travel with an experienced local driver, start early and keep spare days. Check current status before you travel. Do not walk under loose cliffs after heavy rain.

faqs.q: Which flowers grow in Kyongnosla?
faqs.a: Rhododendrons in spring, then from May to August primulas, irises, aconites, potentillas, asters, ground orchids and wild strawberries, among others. The mix changes with altitude and month. A local naturalist can point out species and explain which are rare or poisonous.

faqs.q: Can we collect seeds or plants in Kyongnosla?
faqs.a: No. Kyongnosla is a protected sanctuary, and collecting plants, seeds or flowers is illegal. Some species, such as aconites, are also highly poisonous. Photograph them instead. Buy legal plants and orchids from licensed nurseries in Gangtok if you want to take something home.

experiences.title: Red panda habitat: what to expect
experiences.duration: Built into a birding or nature morning
experiences.image_query: red panda Himalayan Zoological Park Gangtok
experiences.summary: Kyongnosla's lower bamboo thickets are red panda habitat, but the animal is shy and rarely seen. An honest guide to your chances, and where in Gangtok you can see one for sure.
body: The red panda is Sikkim's state animal, a russet, ringed-tailed tree-dweller of temperate bamboo and fir forest. Kyongnosla's dense bamboo at the lower edge of the sanctuary is the kind of forest it needs, and forest records note it here. That does not mean you will see one: red pandas are solitary, active mainly at dawn and dusk, and spend much of their time in trees.

A local guide on an early birding morning will scan likely trees, but treat any sighting as a rare bonus. Stay quiet, keep to the road edge and never use calls or food to attract wildlife. If you do see one, keep your distance and do not follow it.

To see red pandas for certain, visit the Himalayan Zoological Park at Bulbuley near Ganesh Tok in Gangtok, where they live in large forested enclosures. Seeing them there first will help you recognise the habitat at Kyongnosla.

faqs.q: Can we see red pandas in Kyongnosla?
faqs.a: It is possible but rare. Kyongnosla's bamboo thickets are red panda habitat, yet the animals are shy, mostly active at dawn and dusk and usually high in trees. Treat a sighting as a bonus. For a certain view, visit the Himalayan Zoological Park in Gangtok.

faqs.q: Is the red panda Sikkim's state animal?
faqs.a: Yes. The red panda is Sikkim's state animal, and the blood pheasant is its state bird. Both live in the temperate and sub-alpine forests of the state, including Kyongnosla, Fambong Lho and Khangchendzonga National Park. Gangtok's zoo keeps red pandas in forested enclosures.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to see a red panda near Gangtok?
faqs.a: The Himalayan Zoological Park at Bulbuley, opposite Ganesh Tok, about 7 km from MG Marg, keeps red pandas in large wooded enclosures. Go in the morning, when they are more active. In the wild, sightings in Kyongnosla or Fambong Lho are rare and need a guide and luck.

faqs.q: Where is Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary?
faqs.a: It lies on the road from Gangtok to Tsomgo Lake, starting about 31 km from Gangtok, and wraps around the area near the lake. It covers about 31 sq km at roughly 3,290–4,120 m. Most visitors pass through it on the Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La day trip.

faqs.q: Do we need a separate permit for Kyongnosla?
faqs.a: For the road, no: the Tsomgo protected-area permit covers driving through. For walks into the forest or birding off the road, you need permission from the Sikkim forest department and a local guide. Check current status before you travel; we arrange both on request.

faqs.q: When was Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary established?
faqs.a: It was established in 1977, making it one of Sikkim's older protected areas. It is part of the Sacred Himalayan Landscape conservation corridor, and BirdLife lists it, together with Tsomgo and the Cho La area, as an Important Bird Area.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kyongnosla?
faqs.a: Mid-April to late May for rhododendrons, May to August for alpine ground flowers, and November to April for birding, especially the blood pheasant. October and November give the clearest skies. June to September brings monsoon cloud and landslide risk on the road.

faqs.q: Can we trek in Kyongnosla?
faqs.a: Short walks with forest department permission and a local guide are possible, but there are no marked tourist trails. The terrain is steep and high, above 3,000 m, so only fit, acclimatised walkers should try. For longer treks, look at Fambong Lho or the Dzongri route in West Sikkim.

faqs.q: Is Kyongnosla suitable for children?
faqs.a: Seeing it from the car on the Tsomgo trip is fine for children. Long walks at over 3,000 m are not advisable for young children. Keep them warm, give them water and snacks, and watch for signs of altitude sickness, such as headache, vomiting or unusual tiredness.

faqs.q: Which animals live in Kyongnosla?
faqs.a: The sanctuary is habitat for the red panda, Himalayan monal, blood pheasant and other high-altitude birds, as well as smaller mammals. Most animals are shy and rarely seen from the road. Birds are the most visible, especially on early winter mornings with a guide.

faqs.q: How much does a Kyongnosla birding trip cost?
faqs.a: Expect about ₹4,500–6,500 for a reserved car for the Tsomgo road day, plus ₹2,000–3,500 for a local birding guide for a half day, and the usual Tsomgo permit fees of about ₹200–400 per person. Prices are indicative and vary with season.

faqs.q: Is there anywhere to eat in Kyongnosla?
faqs.a: There are a few tea stalls along the Tsomgo road and many more at the lake itself. For early birding trips, carry hot drinks and breakfast from Gangtok. Do not leave food or wrappers in the forest; take all rubbish back with you.
